translations.text: The life and conduct of the holy and honored ascetic fathers Apa Longinus and Apa Lucius, his spiritual father.
They completed their honored lives on the second day of the month of Meshir, in the peace of God. Amen.
As for those who have perfected ways of life suited to people clothed in flesh, let tongues of flesh speak their praises.

But those whose way of life has surpassed the human measure, and whose achievements have risen above the burden borne by those clothed in flesh, almost as though they had no flesh upon them—what tongue of flesh can declare the honor due to them?
People like these need the tongues of bodiless beings to speak their praises, in keeping with the angelic lives they have perfected.

The burden of the flesh did not prevent them in any way from becoming equal to the angels and fulfilling the way of life of those in heaven while they were on earth, according to what the holy apostle said:
“Our citizenship is in heaven, from where we await our Savior, our Lord, who will transform our lowly condition into the likeness of his glorious body.”
For this reason, when I wished to write down the history of Saint Apa Longinus and his spiritual father, Apa Lucius,
who perfected their ways of life—not to mention their contests and struggles—I was inwardly at a loss, knowing my own weakness and the greatness of that saint’s virtues.
Like someone standing beneath an exceedingly high rock and attempting to scale that rock or climb up it, I was at a loss on every side, wondering how I could possibly climb to the top of that rock.
Allow me to say that the rock is Christ. For wherever the saints are, the Lord of the saints is there.
For he who did not hesitate to go up into the mountains with Peter and John did not hesitate to dwell with Apa Longinus and Apa Lucius, his father, in the place where they were.
And perhaps, just as that vision showed Peter and John who it was who had gone up onto that rock,
so too he taught Apa Lucius and Apa Longinus the upright faith, which many attained through them, as we will explain as we proceed.
Nevertheless, knowing my own weaknesses, I wanted to remain silent about the history of those saints because of their greatness and my own insignificance,
although I also saw judgment before my eyes, threatening me in this way: “Does cowardice of this kind really please God?
If you truly acknowledge that they are saints and worthy of praise, and that their ways of life have reached such heights as you describe,
and that their life can build up those who hear it, why do you choose silence instead of telling us the life of those saints?
Even if you cannot tell us about the way of life of those saints, which is filled with every virtue, at least tell humbly what you can grasp, so that you will not be
as though you begrudged the benefit to the souls of those who will hear the life of that holy and praiseworthy man and imitate them in some small measure.
Especially since the herald of truth, the teacher Paul, commands:
‘Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. As you consider the excellence of their conduct, imitate their faith.’

And since God knew that they would benefit those who would hear about the lives of people who lived according to his will, he wrote down for us through his Holy Spirit the lives of the patriarchs and all the other saints

—those who lived under the old covenant and the new—not so that we would merely hear about them, but so that, by imitating their manner of life, we too would inherit the promises God made to those who love him.”
So, as I reflected on these things in my heart, I considered it necessary to begin the account of the saints and to remind you of their way of life, knowing with certainty that:
“The memory of the righteous is a good memory,” and that “A good report gladdens the heart.”
Especially because people rejoice when speaking of the righteous, according to what the wise Solomon said.
The conduct and life of our holy father Apa Longinus, who was from the monastic settlement of the Enaton near Alexandria.
He was a man of this kind. By his earthly ancestry, he came from a city in Lycia,
but he was a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem, with his citizenship in heaven, according to the words of the wise Paul.
While he was still a little boy, he came to love the philosophy of the monastic life and set out for a monastery in his own region of Lycia, called the monastery of Apa Hieronicus.
When he was found worthy to receive the holy monastic habit in that monastery, he was entrusted to a great ascetic named Apa Lucius,
who was adorned with the teaching of the holy Scriptures and with discernment, the mother of all virtues.
He also instructed him in the faith and in all the observances appropriate to the monastic life.

After he had spent some time living in the monastery and practicing the virtues of Christ—humility, gentleness, renunciation, and the other virtues like these—the superior of that monastery passed away.
He had been a quiet and peaceable man. Another man was appointed in his place. Then a disturbance arose in the monastery’s congregation for this reason:
They all knew Apa Lucius, and they all looked to him as the one who would lead them after the man who had fallen asleep.
When the holy man realized that a disturbance was likely to arise on his account,
he chose to withdraw from their presence—that is, to leave that monastery and live in solitude [?]. Above all, he never stopped pursuing humility, like his Lord.
As he considered these things, he called his disciple Apa Longinus and said to him, “My son, we know that it is a serious thing to leave our monastery while we are still alive.

But so that we do not become responsible for such a disturbance and bring judgment upon ourselves, I think it is better for us to withdraw to a place by ourselves, according to what is written in Proverbs:
‘It is better to live in a corner of a roof than to live in a new house with rooms plastered with strife.’
So it is better for us to withdraw to a place by ourselves and devote ourselves to the salvation of our souls, for whose sake we renounced the world and everything in it,
rather than remain here and watch the ruin of our monastery.” This was the reason they left their monastery.

Rather, it happened through God’s providence, so that he might reveal the gracious gifts of his goodness, which cares for bodies and our souls through his chosen ones, and so that many might be saved through them.
After leaving their monastery, they reached a quiet village in that same region of Lycia. They settled in a church in that village named after the holy and honored martyr Theoctistus.
This, too, did not happen merely by chance, but so that God’s wonders might be revealed,
just as this was made clear through the meaning of the honored name of the martyr Theoctistus,
which foretold what would happen in his place of prayer through these holy men. For Theoctistus is translated as:
which was built by God. As those saints were built up in the martyr’s name through their ascetic practices and their many struggles,
they in turn built up many souls through the miracles and healings that God worked through them in that place.
When they settled in that place, many people came from the surrounding region, bringing the sick, especially those afflicted by unclean spirits,
and laying them in that cemetery. They received healing through the prayers of that saint.
For there was a woman afflicted by an extremely powerful unclean spirit.
She caused great disturbances and turmoil because of the demon within her, so that she tore the clothes and even the bodies of anyone who approached her.

When they brought her before the servants of God and begged them to pray over her so that she might receive healing through their intercession, she began convulsing again and attacking those around her.
Then she fell at their feet and remained there, being thrown about by the evil spirit that was with her, and foaming at the mouth.
After she cried out in a loud voice, she became like the dead.
Then the blessed Lucius took pity on her and began to pray and lay his hands on her. He instructed his disciple Longinus to pray as well, to place his hands on her, and to seal her.
When they did this, the demon immediately came out of her. She rose like someone waking from sleep, cleansed of the affliction that had been with her.
And so she served the sick in the martyr’s shrine from that day until her death.
This, then, was the first sign that God worked through them after they left the monastery and settled in that church.
I will also tell of another miracle that God performed through his servants.
There was a man in that region who had a son of noble birth who had reached childhood.
There was also a woman named Flavia who entrusted a document to that child’s parents. They gave it to their son to keep safe.
It happened that the child died suddenly, and his parents did not know where the document was.
That woman, Flaviana, came asking for what she had deposited—the document she had entrusted to them. They were at a loss and could not find it, because they did not know where the child had put it.
She threatened them in great anger, saying that she would make them her slaves if they did not return her document to her. When these blessed men heard these things—
Then the child’s parents, as they continued to be harassed by that woman, left their son without burying him and hurried to the place where the saints were, with other large crowds following them,
namely their relatives and their neighbors. They fell at the feet of Father Lucius and Father Longinus,
begging them and saying, “Plead with the Lord Christ, whose servants you are, so that he may make the soul of our son who died appear,
so that we may learn from him where he put the document
that a rich woman entrusted to us. She is now threatening to make us her slaves if we do not find the document and give it to her.”
When the blessed men heard these things from the child’s parents, they took pity on them through the love and compassion of Christ that was within them.
They got up quickly and followed them without any agitation or timidity.

When they reached the house where the little boy lay dead, they went into the place where the dead boy was lying, knelt down, and prayed, since God wished to reveal a miracle through the blessed Apa Longinus, who was full of virtue.
Immediately he was filled with the Holy Spirit. He took the little boy by the hand in front of the crowd and said:
“The God who raised Lazarus in those days will now restore your spirit to you, so that you can tell us where you put the rich woman’s document, so that she will not take your parents as slaves.”
Immediately the little boy’s spirit returned to him. He rose, sat up, and opened his mouth. With everyone standing there listening, he told them where the document was kept in the house.
His parents also asked him about other matters they did not know about, and he answered them about everything they asked him. Then he immediately fell asleep again.
When the people of Lycia saw this miraculous deed that had taken place through the saints, they glorified God, who alone performs these wonders.

As word about them spread through that region, all the people brought them those of their own who were suffering from every kind of illness, so that they would pray over them and heal them. They also bestowed great honors on them.

When they grew weary of the immense crowd that troubled them and of the honor being given to them—which was not hidden from them because of their great humility—they decided to slip away secretly and leave those districts.
But when those living around them realized this, they kept watch over them, since they did not want to be deprived of their blessing and their presence among them.
For they were the pride of that entire region because of the many miracles taking place through them.
Then the blessed Lucius took his disciple aside and said to him, “We cannot go on like this, bearing the empty praise of people. It is no benefit to our souls either.
So, my son, listen to me: get up secretly and go to Alexandria. I have heard about a monastery west of that city called the Enaton, where there is great stillness
in accordance with God’s will. Look for a man from Corinth named Gaius, who is abbot of his own monastery, which he built there, and remain inside with him.
I hope in the Lord God our Savior that, wherever you may be, he will not deprive me of being with you in the body.

Even if some time passes while I am away from you, I trust in the Lord that I will certainly come to you, so that we may finish our race together in the place the Lord will appoint for us according to his will.
Wherever you are, my son, flee from the empty praise of people. Go first to the shrine of Saint Menas and pray. Then go to the Enaton and stay in Apa Gaius’s monastery.”
After he had said these things, they prayed and embraced one another, and so he departed from him.
When the blessed Apa Longinus arrived in Alexandria, he looked for Apa Gaius’s monastery in the Enaton, and some devout people showed him the way to it.
When he reached the monastery, he knocked gently at the door. When the doorkeeper opened the door, he asked him:
“Where are you from, and why have you come here?” Apa Longinus, who was truly humble, answered:
“I am from the region of Lycia, and I have come here to become a monk.” For in his great humility he could not bear to call himself a monk.
He wore neither a hood nor a shoulder wrap, for it was not the custom of foreign monks to wear such things,
but only a sleeveless tunic, a cloak, and a belt. These were what he himself was wearing when he came to the monastery.
For his hair had grown a little because of the many days he had spent on the journey by which he had come.
For this reason they did not immediately recognize that he was a monk. The doorkeeper said to him, “You will not be able to live as a monk here.
For our prescribed psalm-singing is extensive, and our eating, our sleeping, and the rest of our activities involve great hardship and toil.
There is no comfort in them. So take some loaves as a blessing for yourself. The Lord be with you.”
But the noble Apa Longinus did not argue or say a word to him. Instead, when he heard the mention of a blessing, he accepted the loaves with the blessing.

He patiently remained at the entrance for many days, imitating in this respect too the great Anthony, who went to the great Paul the hermit after enduring the great hardship of the journey through the deserts.

That great man did not receive him immediately. But blessed Anthony himself waited patiently at the entrance, saying, “I have sought and I have found, and I believe that the door will be opened to me.”
This man too, since the same Spirit dwelt in him, kept these things in mind and patiently remained at the entrance until, through his great perseverance, he obtained what he had in mind.
As the doorkeeper continued to come out each day to perform his assigned duties, he would find him sitting at the entrance with great patience.
He brought word to the superior of the monastery, saying, “There is a young stranger at the entrance to the monastery. He has been there for several days now, saying,
‘I want to become a monk.’ I have turned him away many times, but he has persevered until now.” The superior answered,
“Since you have seen his perseverance, bring him inside the gate with you, and let him stay and help you with your duties, doing whatever work you assign him.”
Then the doorkeeper brought him inside the gate, as the father of the monastery had commanded.
Not only did he do everything the doorkeeper instructed him to do, but whenever any of the brothers gave him an order, he carried it out with great eagerness and complete obedience.
He persevered in this way at such tasks for two years or more, and he never told the brothers that he was a monk.
But God, who always honors those who honor him, who reveals hidden things and raises up the humble, who said with his truthful mouth,

“People do not light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket. Instead, they put it on the lampstand, so that it gives light to everyone in the house”—did not want his chosen one to remain hidden, but
revealed him as one who truly gives light. He placed him on the spiritual lampstand so that he would give light not only to those around him but also to others far away from him.
He shone upon them through his abundant fruit and his virtuous deeds, as the narrative will reveal to us as the account proceeds.
There was a merchant from Lycia, Apa Longinus’s homeland, who knew him well while he was still in his monastery. It happened that he came to Alexandria on business.
When he went to the sanctuary of Saint Menas to pray, he also wanted to go, as was his custom, to the monastery of the blessed priest Gaius,
since he had great faith in that place. When he came to him to receive his blessing, he asked him to pray for him.
While he was sitting at the entrance to the church, Saint Gaius spoke many words of instruction to him from the holy Scriptures for the salvation of his soul.
The merchant looked and saw Apa Longinus, who had raised the dead man and performed many miracles in the region of Lycia. Yet he doubted, thinking, “It is not him, but someone who looks like him.”
For his hair had grown long over time, and he was in a very wretched condition. For this reason the merchant did not recognize him with certainty.
There had been a mark on his face since his childhood. When the merchant looked closely at the mark on his face, he said to Saint Gaius:
“You have a great man here in this monastery who has performed many miracles.”
The superior said to him, “Which of the brothers are you saying this about?” The merchant said to him, “I am speaking about the man sweeping by the gate.”
“For this is Apa Longinus, who became famous in the region of Lycia, together with his spiritual father, Apa Lucius.
He raised the dead and drove many demons out of people, and God worked many other healings through him in that region.
So when his fame spread throughout that region and everyone honored him,
he left his spiritual father behind, fled, and came here secretly, escaping the empty praise of people.”
While he was saying these things about Saint Apa Longinus, Longinus was sweeping in the gateway.
Then the abbot called him and said to him, “Why did you hide yourself from us and not tell us that you were a monk?”
Immediately Apa Longinus, who was truly humble in his heart, fell at the feet of Gaius the priest and bowed before him, saying, “Forgive me, my father.”
At once the superior ordered that the hair which had grown on his head be shaved off. He prayed over him and dressed him in the hood and cloak according to the monastic habit of Alexandria.
When the brothers in the monastery heard all these things about Apa Longinus, they regarded him as a great and spiritually mature man, and they began to honor him even more.
But when Saint Apa Longinus saw that people were honoring him, he was distressed,
and he remembered all the more the instruction his spiritual father had given him: “Flee from the empty praise of people.”
Then he considered the matter within himself, saying, “I left my homeland because of people's praise, and I parted from my father.
How can I stay here when such a great crowd is honoring me?”
For this reason he left that monastery. Some God-loving people built him a small cell nearby, beside the sea.
He lived there in solitude, making cords. He toiled at his manual work so that he would have the means to give to those in need from the work of his hands,
imitating in this the holy apostle Paul, who says, “These hands provided for my needs and for those who were with me,” and, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
Many prominent shipowners would come to him and take the cords he made with his holy hands, arranging them in the shape of a cross
in the middle of their sails as a blessing. They believed that his prayers would be a strong protection for them and that the Lord would keep their ships safe wherever they went.
After a few days, three monks came to him and became his disciples.
One night, as he was sitting with his disciples, meditating on the word of God and doing manual work,
he dozed while sitting on his seat in the place where he worked, remembering the words of the holy psalmist David:
“I will not give sleep to my eyes, slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, [?] a place for the Lord, a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.”
[?] While he was sitting at night, sleep overcame him, and he fell into a trance. A man appeared to be standing before him, saying to him:
“Get up quickly and go to the seashore. There you will find your father, Apa Lucius. He has come to you from the countryside.”
He got up immediately, without telling any of his disciples, and went to the shore of the sea, to the place he had been told about in the revelation.
He found the holy Apa Lucius, who had just arrived by boat. When they had greeted one another, the old man said to him:
“Did I not tell you, my son, that I trust in Christ that wherever you go, I will come to you?”
Then they gave glory to God because he had made them worthy to see one another, and because what was written had been fulfilled:

“The deer gathered there and saw one another’s faces. They came out in full number; not one of them was missing. For it was the Lord who commanded them, and it was his Spirit who gathered them together.”
For the great trumpet of the prophets rightly called such people deer, since deer love the wilderness and pursue the race of snakes as enemies.

This, in turn, is how these holy men behave: they flee from the turmoil of the cities and live in deserted places. They also constantly pursue the race of spiritual snakes, which are the spirits of wickedness.
The two of them walked on and went inside together. His disciples were sitting, reciting and working.
When they saw the holy Apa Longinus walking with his father, they were amazed. They rose with great joy and greeted one another. After praying, they sat down.
Apa Longinus said to them, “This is your father from this day onward.” Then he told them what he had done to them in the vision concerning him.
The holy Apa Lucius had Apa Longinus teach him too how to make [?].
From then on they continued serving God with great devotion, living together in great peace, each keeping to his assigned place in every service,
so that the fame of their conduct and their sober way of life filled the great city of Alexandria and all Egypt.
For there was a woman with a disease in her breast, which physicians call cancer.
She had heard about the great Apa Longinus, that the Lord performed healings through him. She rose in faith and set out.
When she reached the seashore, she encountered the holy Apa Longinus splitting wood beside the sea, as was his custom. She asked him:
“Where is God’s servant, Apa Longinus?” He said, “What do you want with him?”
She told him about the disease she had. He said to her, “What do you want with that man? He is nothing.”
Then he made the sign of the cross over the diseased part of her body, saying, “May my Lord Jesus Christ deal with you according to your faith.”
The woman believed and set off for home. When she had gone a short distance from him, she was cured of the disease.
When she entered the city, she told everyone about the healing she had received through the holy man. They asked her, “What does that man look like?”
She described the features of his blessed face, and they told her that it was Apa Longinus who had healed her. The woman gave glory to God.
Oh, who can recount the healings and wonders that God performed through him? If I wished to speak of each one of his healings, time would fail me while I was still speaking.
But I will tell a few of them and bring this account to an end here, holding back so that some people do not become unbelieving because of the great number of miracles.

For many people came to him from the city of Alexandria and its surrounding districts, wanting to find the place where he was. They brought him everyone suffering from every kind of illness, and he healed them all.
One day a woman brought him her son, who had a demon. His face had been twisted backward by the demon’s power, and it threw him down every day, tormenting him.
His mother begged the holy man to pray over him. He stretched out his hands and prayed, saying:
“Lord Jesus Christ, you who work for our salvation, if it is your will, grant healing to this little boy.” As he did this, he breathed into the little boy’s face.
Immediately the demon came out of him, and his face became as it had been before. They hurried home, glorifying God.
When they saw that many people were coming to them, they found it necessary to bake some small loaves for their own needs and those of the strangers and visitors who came to them.
While the loaves were spread out in the sun, a heavy downpour of rain suddenly poured down. Immediately the holy man, Apa Longinus, stood up and prayed, saying:
“God of all and maker of creation, command this deadly rainstorm to pass us by.”
Immediately the clouds moved away from that place where the loaves were, and not a single drop fell on the loaves,
for his prayer had become like a shelter over the place where the loaves were. Not a single drop fell on the loaves.
On another occasion, he was sitting in his cell, working on [?] and meditating on the word of God,
when a woman came to him suffering from a disease in her hand, which doctors call “amianton,” meaning incurable.
She came behind the cell and begged him, saying, “Please be so kind as to pray over me.” But he sternly ordered her to go away.

She stayed there silently, afraid to speak. But when he learned through the Spirit of the great suffering she was enduring, he got up and closed the window opening through which she was looking in. He said to her:
“Go in peace. The Lord grants you healing.” And the woman was healed from that very moment.
One day a man came to receive something from him and begged him to give him a cowl of his, so that it might be a source of help to him.
When he had received it, he left him. When he went home, there was a man there who had a demon upon him.
When he saw the man holding Apa Longinus’s cowl, the demon threw him to the ground, and he cried out, saying:
“Why have you brought Apa Longinus here to persecute people?” Those in the house were astonished at what the demon was saying.
The man was amazed and realized that these things had happened because of Apa Longinus’s cowl. Immediately he took it and laid it on the demon-possessed man, saying:
“In the name of the God [?] of my father Apa Longinus, come out of him!” And immediately the demon came out of him.
When the people saw what had happened, they glorified God, who performs these miracles through his saints.
Another day, while he was sitting, the elders belonging to the monastic settlement were sitting beside him, having come to visit him. While they were talking about the welfare of their souls,
he suddenly got up as though someone had called him. He came out of the cell and went to the harbor. He found a boat that had come from the south, with a holy elder aboard it.
When the old man saw him, he greeted him with a holy kiss. Then the old man raised his eyes to heaven and said:
“Lord, did I not beg you, ‘Do not let this holy man know that I am coming to him, so that he will not trouble himself and come out to meet me’?” He turned to Abba Longinus and said to him:
“My time to leave this life has drawn near. That is why the Lord sent me to you, so that you might lay your hands over my eyes.”
So the two of them walked on and entered Abba Longinus’s cell. After three days the old man passed away at a good old age.
With the holy Abba Longinus laying his hand over his eyes, he completed his life at a good old age.
On another occasion, he was entering the cell of one of his disciples, whose name was Arcadius. Arcadius was working on a [?] and had nearly finished it. Abba Longinus said to him:
“My son Arcadius, hurry and finish it, because God is about to send for you now.”
When he had finished the [?], he took him by the hand, stretched him out on the mat, and turned his face toward the east. Immediately the disciple peacefully gave his spirit into God’s hands.
One day they brought him a man possessed by a demon and begged him to drive it out of him. Abba Longinus, however, said to him with humility of heart:
“I do not know what [?] for him. But go instead to Abba Zeno, and I trust in God that he will grant him healing.”
When they went to Abba Zeno, they begged him to pray over him. When Abba Zeno began to pray, the demon cried out:
“Do you think I am coming out because of you? No! Look, Abba Longinus is over there praying, and I am coming out because I am afraid of his prayers. Otherwise I would not answer you.”
When the unclean spirit had said this, it came out of the man. There was also a disciple of his who had done some improper things.
When Abba Theodore of the Enaton learned of this, he came to him with some other elders. They begged him to send the disciple away from him.

But he would not listen to them, because perhaps the disciple would repent and God would forgive him—God, who does not desire the sinner’s death so much as that he should repent and live. He only said this one thing to them:
“Woe to us! We renounce the world and enter this monastic life, saying that we will become like the angels, yet instead we become worse than the unclean spirits.”
One day a prominent shipowner also came to him, bringing a very large sum of money to give him.
But he took nothing from him, saying, “We do not need anything of this kind. The work of our own human hands is enough for us.

But please mount your donkey and hurry to the landing place of Saint Peter. You will find a man there wearing clothes of a certain kind and with other marks on his face—God has just revealed these things to me. Ask him:
‘Where are you going, and what is that you have with you?’” The shipowner hurried off as the old man had instructed.
When he reached the landing place, he found the man Abba Longinus had told him about. He approached him and spoke to him.
But the man gave him no answer at all because of the distress he was in. Instead, he was hurrying to leave the city and do what he had in mind.
When the shipowner saw his agitation and how troubled he was, he said to him, “I have just come from the Enaton, from my father Abba Longinus.
He is the one who sent me to you.” When the man heard Abba Longinus’s name, he stopped. The shipowner gave him the money.
The man told him about his distress, saying, “I owe many debts, and the creditors are putting pressure on me over them, [?] pay them.”
I decided to go outside the city and hang myself because of the many troubles weighing on me. And so that you may know the truth, here is the rope in my hand with which I am going to hang myself.
And he showed him the rope he was holding. The shipowner was amazed at Apa Longinus’s words. He gave the gold to the man and went home.
The shipowner returned to Apa Longinus and told him everything that had happened. The old man said to him:
Believe me, my son, if we had neglected this even a little longer, God would have judged us both for that man’s soul.
At that time, when Emperor Marcian wanted to send an imperial official to Alexandria with the Tome of the impious Leo,
he ordered the city of Alexandria to sign it, especially the monks of the Enaton. But he revealed this matter to the holy Apa Longinus three months beforehand,
and in the revelation shown to him, he commanded him to gather all the monks of the Enaton and tell them what had happened.
And he commanded them not to accept that doctrine at all or to sign it.
Apa Longinus himself gathered everyone in the monastic settlement and told them what the Lord had revealed to him in the vision, and
he commanded them to keep the Lord’s ordinances steadfastly and to struggle for the faith of the orthodox even to death.
When they heard these things from Apa Longinus, they rejoiced greatly and consulted with one another, saying:
No one will be able to put an end to this defiled doctrine except the man to whom the Lord revealed this mystery, telling him about the trouble destined to come.
Then they begged the blessed Apa Longinus to become their father and guide and the abbot over the monasteries of the Enaton.
After three months, the imperial official arrived with that godless doctrine,
the emperor having written to Acacius, the Augustal prefect who was governing at that time, to compel the monks in the monastic settlement to sign Leo’s defiled Tome. The duke,
when he read the emperor’s letter, copied it onto a writing tablet and sent it to the monks of the Enaton. It was written as follows:
Acacius, the Augustal prefect, writes to the holy, God-loving fathers, the monks of the monastic settlement of the Enaton: Greetings.
Since our lord, the sovereign emperor, has deemed us worthy of his sacred letter,
directing everyone to sign the Tome of Leo, bishop of Rome, and especially Your Holinesses,
O monks of the Enaton, now, when you receive the letter from the imperial official, you are to carry out
the command of our lord the emperor, so that you may receive gifts and honors from the great benefactor and sovereign who fights for our wisdom.
When the holy Apa Longinus received the letter, he gathered all the brothers and read the writing tablet to them.
When they heard it, they cried out together, pronouncing anathema on that defiled doctrine and its contents, on the impious Leo, and on everyone in communion with him.
Then they wrote a letter to the Augustal prefect in these terms: You, for your part, are subject to the emperor’s defiled doctrine.
But we, for our part, submit to the Almighty, who benefits all things through his providence.
Let Your Excellency therefore know that none of us, from the least to the greatest, will tolerate sharing in, or even listening at all to, that filthy doctrine of the lawless and ungodly Leo.
Instead, we are all ready to struggle to the death for the established doctrines and traditions of the sound faith of our holy and orthodox fathers, which they handed down to us.
We need not write you many words, for it is better for us and beneficial to our souls to obey the decree of the Almighty rather than that of your emperor.
When the governor received the letter and understood its force, he and the emperor’s official became extremely angry at the defense offered by the holy men of the Enaton.
They consulted together and decided that the imperial official should take the troops and kill the monks of the Enaton.
But the Lord, who frustrates the plans of rulers, revealed this to the holy elders, Apa Lucius and Apa Longinus.
They gathered all the brothers together, and Apa Longinus said to them, “I beg you, brothers, do not let any one of you become alarmed.
Instead, listen to me. Let each of you take some branches from the palm trees, and let us all go together to meet the governor before he comes to us.”
This proposal pleased the brothers. They took palm branches and went to the place called Lithazomenon, outside the city.
The whole company of monks stood there. No one dared to enter the city, because this was their father’s command.
Then the imperial official came to wage war against the monks. When they reached them, he ordered the troops to shoot arrows at the company of monks.
The soldiers shot arrows at them. Oh, what a great wonder! The soldiers stood shooting at the company of monks, yet not one of them was harmed.
And they all sang this hymn together with one voice, saying, “We have put our trust in the Lord. How can you say to our soul, ‘Flee to the mountains like a sparrow’?
For look, the sinners have drawn their bows and prepared their arrows on the bowstring to shoot in secret at those who are upright in heart.”
And again, “The sinners have drawn their swords and bent their bows to bring down the poor and needy and slaughter those who are upright in heart.”
Truly, their swords entered their own hearts, and their arrows were broken. But the mighty soldier, Apa Longinus, was the one who fought for the truth to the death,
the one who showed that he himself dwelt under the shadow of the Most High. He was not afraid of the arrows flying through the air, but took the confession of faith as a shield, saying:
“His truth will surround you like armor. You will not be afraid of an arrow flying by day.”
As the mighty elder meditated on these words, he advanced toward the troops with great courage, even though they were shooting arrows.
The arrows were flying on either side of him, but not one of them touched the brave man.
When the imperial official saw his great courage, he was amazed that none of the arrows had touched him and that none of the brothers had been harmed at all.
They immediately dismounted from their horses, fell at Apa Longinus’s feet, and bowed before him and the brothers with him, asking forgiveness for the reckless deed they had committed.
When Apa Longinus saw their repentance and faith, he spoke to the imperial official and the soldiers, saying:
“Look, you have seen that we have struggled and prepared ourselves to fight to the death for the faith of the fathers.
We invite you to come to the monastery of the Enaton, where our fathers are, so that we may question them in Your Excellency’s presence, to give you full assurance.”
And whatever they command us in your presence, we are ready to obey their word.
But the brothers were puzzled by the words Apa Longinus was speaking before the governor and the troops, and they said to one another:
“Did any of us remain in the monastery without coming here?” Then they approached their father Apa Longinus, saying:
“Our father, do you not know that we are all here, and not one of us is outside? How can we trouble these men and inconvenience them by making them come to the monastery?”
But he gave them no answer, since he knew what he was going to do. Then they all followed him—the imperial official and all the brothers.
He walked ahead of them until he brought them to the tombs containing the bones of their fathers, the elders who had lived before him,
who had firmly maintained the sound faith until the end of their lives, in accordance with what pleased God.
Then he stood among the tombs, stretched out his hands, and prayed. He also instructed them to pray with him. When he finished the prayer, they all said “Amen” together.
Apa Longinus opened his mouth and raised his voice before them, saying:
“My holy fathers, is it indeed God’s will that we accept Leo’s doctrine and sign it?”
Immediately a voice came from the tombs containing the bodies of the saints, saying three times:
“A curse on the doctrine of the godless Leo! Do not utter his name with your mouths, nor have communion with anyone who accepts that doctrine.
A curse on those who sign Leo’s Tome, the blasphemies of Leo!
For it is full of blasphemy against the divinity of Christ, dividing it into two natures after the union of Christ.”
When the imperial official and all the troops accompanying them heard that voice coming from among the bodies of the saints, they were amazed
beyond measure. They fell at the feet of Apa Longinus and the other monks with him, asking them to grant them forgiveness and pray for them, so that they might come to the knowledge of the truth.

Immediately many of the troops renounced their military service and the affairs of this empty life. They became monks and placed themselves under the authority of the holy Apa Longinus because of the fear that had come over them.
But the imperial official and the remaining soldiers returned to the city, recounting the wonders they had seen.

When the people of the city heard about the miracles and wonders that had taken place through Apa Longinus, they became even firmer in the faith, and together they rushed to the governor’s headquarters.
They brought out Acacius, the Augustal prefect, who was forcing them to accept communion with Leo’s Tome, and burned him in the middle of the city.
But I say that they did not simply subject him to such a disgraceful death for no reason. Rather, it was a sentence of God’s judgment through the mouth of the great Apa Longinus
and the brothers with him, in accordance with a prophecy that our king David uttered in the tenth psalm, singing in this way:
“Fire and a storm are the portion of their cup.” But when the bishop of that heresy saw the disturbance that had taken place,
he changed his appearance, put on secular clothing, and left the city. He fled because of the fear that had come over him, and he has not been found to this day.
The church spoke boldly through the doctrines of the orthodox faith, and it advanced daily through the intercession of the Holy Spirit.
After this struggle, which the blessed Apa Longinus endured, he spent another twenty years governing the monasteries
of the laura. He was deemed worthy to lay his hands over the eyes of his father, Apa Lucius, just as Joseph laid his hands over the eyes of his father Jacob.
Apa Longinus shepherded the brothers with complete understanding, and he urged them to flee from empty glory, which is the beginning of all the passions.
For empty glory gives rise to the love of money, which is the root of evil.
The love of money gives birth to anger; anger gives birth to pride; anger gives birth to envy, that evil beast.
He also used to teach them to devote themselves diligently to manual work at the proper time and to hold their worship gatherings in the fear of God.
He made himself an example to them in everything, caring for them all, both through bodily nourishment and through the teaching of the Lord.
For he lived among them like a bishop. Everyone who wished to live according to God's law looked to him and set their lives right according to his virtues.
For who hated empty glory as he did? Or who was as exalted in his deeds and as humble in his thoughts as this man?
He was humble in every way, with his face bowed down, conducting himself wisely.
For he did not wear a deceptive religious habit like the people of this age, who outwardly take on the appearance of godliness while inwardly they are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness.
Who was as patient as this man, bearing patiently with those who had stumbled in their transgressions until he restored them once more to their original state?
[?] in this way, he departed to the Lord whom he loved on the second day of Meshir, resting with all his fathers, whom he had resembled in his righteous deeds and his way of life,
namely, the patriarchs, the prophets, the apostles, and all the saints who did the will of God.
Oh, how great was the grief on the day when he went to his rest! Not only the brother monks, but also the city of Alexandria and its districts,
especially those in the surrounding area, cried out loudly and wept because such a father had been taken from them.
Indeed, the sound of their weeping mingled with the hymn they were singing. The old men were looking for the staff of their old age,
the young for the bridle of their self-control, and those who had newly entered a life of obedience were looking for the one who would lead them into the kingdom of heaven.
The married were looking for their lawgiver, the poor for the one who cared for them, and the sick for the one who healed their illnesses, whether of the soul or of the body.
In short, whether they were monks or laypeople, he cared for them all so that they might be saved, presenting them all as holy to the Lord Jesus Christ.
To him be glory, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, who is of the same essence and gives life, now and always, forever and ever. Amen.
